chapters.title: The Milli-Second
chapters.simulation:
I design bridges by talking to a machine. I say a sentence, it hands me three ways to build it, I pick one, I sign my name to load calculations I never ran myself. Nine years since Oxford. Three since I stopped drawing lines by hand. I sleep four hours a night in a city of eleven million, and most of what I feel, I feel in twenty minutes with strangers I pay to be honest with me. Not for the sex. For the second after it. Something leaks through. I call it the glimpse. I've never said that word out loud to anyone.

Her name was Gift, which a third of the women in this city use, the way a third of American men are named Mike. Twenty-six. A photographer's assistant, three photos on the app, one of her actual face and two of her hands doing something with light I couldn't identify and didn't need to. She set her own terms in eleven messages — the room, the hour, the price split down the middle, no negotiation on that, I offered and she said no, we split it, this isn't that. I liked her for the sentence before I liked anything else about her. People who tell you what a thing isn't before you have to guess wrong are rare enough to notice.

Ratchada, a short-time hotel with a gate that swallows your car so nobody driving past sees whose it is. Six hundred eighty baht, three hours, a television the size of a dining table playing a drama with the sound off, a jacuzzi tub neither of us used.

She undressed in one motion, like taking off a decision. She told me what she wanted before I asked — that's the part nobody tells you about the apps, the good ones flip the whole structure. She isn't there to be wanted. She's there wanting something, and you're the instrument that happened to show up on a Tuesday. She held my jaw with one hand, not hard, the way you hold a glass you don't want to spill, and she watched my face the whole time instead of closing her eyes, which almost nobody does. She was somewhere private with her eyes open. I found that more erotic than anything I could have started myself.

Her breath changed first. Then her hands. Then a sound that wasn't a word. I felt her weight shift the way a beam shifts when the load finally reaches the member built to carry it — not collapse, transfer. And in the second after, the one the word millisecond undersells —

I saw a ceiling.

Cream. No source for the light on it, no shadow, the way a shadow needs a direction and this one had none. A chair in the corner of it, gray, wide-armed, the kind you'd sit in for a long procedure, not a short one. Gone before I could turn my head, if turning my head meant anything in whatever position I was actually in.

Third time. Always after. Always brief. Always the ceiling, sometimes the chair.

I asked Gift, after, four inches of hot air between us and the fan doing nothing, if she ever felt like she was somewhere else in that second. She said no. She said she felt more exactly where she was than anywhere else all week, that this was the whole point of a Tuesday instead of something with a name — a name drags you into every other room of your life, this only asks for the one.

I didn't tell her about the ceiling. There's no way to say it that isn't a symptom or a bad line. She got dressed the same way she'd undressed, reversed, one motion, no performance in either direction. She counted out her half, three hundred forty baht, onto the nightstand next to the key without being asked. I offered to walk her to the sky train. She said no thank you, she liked walking alone after, it was part of how she came back to herself, and I understood that completely and felt closer to her in that sentence than in the ninety minutes before it. Anticipation is a kind of architecture too. You build the room the feeling happens in before the feeling arrives, and she'd built hers correctly, for herself, without needing me for it.

A dog eating its dinner doesn't audit the meal. Something in me has civilized itself so far past that dog that I need my body to overwhelm my mind completely, for a second, just so the mind stops asking whether any of it counts — and even then, at the one moment a body is supposed to be unanswerable, mine hands me a ceiling instead of an answer. I don't know if that makes me the most honest animal in the room or the most broken one. I'm not going to pretend I've worked that out.

Driving home, red light on Rama IV, a gray sedan pulled up beside me. Ordinary car. The man driving it looked at me the full two seconds the light allows, the way you look at something you've already decided about and are only confirming. Then it changed and he went right and I went straight and nothing happened. I want to be honest that nothing happened.

I remember his face better than I remember Gift's.

In the garage under my building there was a dent in the passenger door, fist-sized, paint intact, like the car had been leaned on hard by something that didn't want to break the surface, only bend what was under it. I don't remember making it. The dashcam loops every ninety-six hours and showed nothing, which isn't the same as proving nothing happened inside that window. I stood in the garage a long time looking at it, the fluorescent light doing its flat thing, a security camera blinking its small red confirmation in the corner that it was, in fact, recording something, though I've never once seen anyone review that footage or known who could.

Upstairs, showered, one meal — grilled fish, rice — I sat on the balcony with a nicotine pouch, 28 milligrams, tucked against my gum, strong enough that most people spit it out inside ninety seconds. I don't. I've built a tolerance to it the way I've built a tolerance to the two hours after midnight generally, the hour the thoughts stop taking turns and start arriving all at once. My phone lit at 11:52pm. No name. A dash where a photo should be.

—— 02:47 stop testing the edges with your body

I read it four times. I checked the number — unregistered, no country code I could resolve. I typed back a question mark and got nothing. I did not sleep well. I did not expect to.

I got up once, at 1:40, and stood at the sliding door to the balcony without opening it. Twenty-three floors down, Bangkok did what it does at that hour, which is pretend to sleep while half of it works. A 7-Eleven sign burned green on the corner. A motorcycle taxi driver sat on his bike doing nothing, which is its own kind of work, the work of being available. I have never once, in forty-five years, put something down and failed to remember where. I lost myself for eleven minutes once, at six, in a mall that doesn't exist anymore. That's the whole inventory. And now there was a dent I didn't make, in a door I lock every night, and a sentence on my phone from a number that resolves to nowhere, telling me to stop testing the edges of something with a body I had, until that message, considered entirely mine to spend.

chapters.title: The First Video
chapters.simulation:
The phone rang at 3:14am. +43. Vienna. Michael's number.

Michael has been dead since the third of May.

I let it ring out. Six rings, then the specific quiet a call makes when it ends without a voicemail attached. I lay there and counted to sixty. It rang again. Same number. I let that one go too.

I didn't call back. Calling back a dead man's number at 3:14 in the morning is a decision you can't take back, and I've gotten careful about decisions like that.

His last text, April 29th, sits unanswered because I only sent a thumbs up, the coward's punctuation: Good dinner. The ambassador said something I didn't expect. Tell you properly when we talk. We never talked. Four days later he was dead, and whatever the ambassador said folded itself into whatever gets folded away when a person stops being available to unfold it. I have read that text more times than I've read anything Lek ever wrote me, and Lek's handwriting I could recite from memory.

Michael made this city feel like a scene instead of a place to survive. Knew where to eat before the guidebooks did. Had an opinion on every new building and was usually right about which ones would age badly. Bangkok without him in it is a photo with the color balance shifted three degrees toward gray. Nothing you could point to. Everything a little less itself.

I got up, drank water in the dark because turning on a light felt like admitting something, and went back to bed. Didn't sleep.

At 6am I did the vitamins anyway and told the AI to hold the bridge documents till Thursday. It said understood. It has never once asked me why.

I opened LinkedIn at 6:40. His profile came up — same headline, Senior Trade Advisor, Austrian Trade Commission, though a receptionist had told me six weeks back, no hesitation in her voice, that he was "former." Same photo, some gala, 2021, tuxedo, a glass of something amber. Except the photo was soft now. Not pixelated — soft, the way an image goes when you zoom too far in, except I hadn't zoomed at all. I compared it to a screenshot from three weeks earlier. The old one was sharp, every wrinkle at his eye, the grain of the fabric. This one had lost maybe thirty percent of its information. Nobody re-faxes a static image sitting on a server. Photographs don't degrade themselves out of boredom.

I called the number again. Six rings, cut clean, no voicemail, like a landline that ran out of somewhere to send the sound.

I opened my own camera roll and scrolled back to his fifty-fourth birthday, February, a private room at a steakhouse on Convent Road, fourteen people, a bottle of something Australian that cost more than my rent that month. I counted the faces in the group photo twice. Fourteen people, fourteen faces, Michael dead center exactly where the photographer told him to stand, because he was, as always, the reason everyone else had shown up. Nothing wrong with it. I kept looking anyway, the way you press a tooth that doesn't hurt yet, just to confirm it still can.

I went to the office at ten, a generous word for the chair I keep in a coworking space on Thonglor. The AI had three revisions of a pedestrian bridge waiting, unrequested, plus a note: I noticed the load path assumption from Tuesday conflicted with the soil report filed in March. Corrected. Confirm. I confirmed. I thought, not for the first time, that I've built a working relationship with something that catches my mistakes before I've finished making them, and that this should feel like collaboration and mostly feels like being quietly, competently outgrown.

Dao texted at noon. We'd been at Michael's fortieth together, some rooftop with a saxophonist nobody had asked for. I asked if she'd noticed anything strange on his Facebook. She said she hadn't seen his posts in a while. I asked when she unfollowed him. She said she didn't remember unfollowing him at all. She said she wasn't sure she had.

By two I'd walked eleven thousand steps without deciding to, which happens some days, the body doing its assigned work while the mind does something else entirely. I ended up on Sukhumvit 22, outside a dispensary I hadn't planned to visit. Add runs the place, forearms like a man who used to lift for a living. I've been coming since 2022, back when the law said yes, and kept coming after it re-grayed into something nobody fully understands, including the police who enforce it selectively.

"Something for the two hours after midnight," I said, our shorthand. He reached for a jar without checking the label. He weighed it on a scale older than the shop and said, without looking up, "You look like a man checking a corpse's pulse to see if it changed its mind."

I asked what that meant.

"Nothing. My brother went to Chiang Mai for a retreat six years ago and never really came all the way back. Not dead. Thinned out. Still answers the phone. Doesn't sound like him."

I didn't tell him about Michael. I watched the scale settle instead, the little digital numbers ticking down toward the exact gram, and thought about 2022, when this whole street legalized overnight and every shophouse for three blocks sprouted a green cross like a fever breaking, and how within eighteen months the government re-grayed the law into something nobody, including the police who enforce it selectively, can fully explain without contradicting the sentence before it. A thing can be legal, illegal, and simply tolerated, all three at once, in the same country, in the same week. I paid twelve hundred baht, cash, and walked out with contraband an entire industry pretends not to notice.

The video arrived at 9:41pm. I was on the balcony, the city doing its evening thing below.

—— 02:47 [video attached] you already know what this is about

The timestamp said 02:47. My phone's clock said 9:41. I sat with that for a full minute before opening it.

Four minutes eleven seconds. A voice, flat, unhurried, the cadence people use for things they consider obviously true. It described a universe with no author behind it, no ledger, no floor beneath the floor. It didn't argue. It described, the way weather gets described — a condition, not a position.

I watched it twice. The second time I caught something under the narration, three seconds in — a sound like a chair adjusting under weight. Then nothing. Then the voice continuing like the interruption never happened.

I called Neung. He picked up on the fourth ring, television loud behind him, one of the Chinese dramas our mother used to watch dubbed badly into Thai. I didn't tell him about the video. I asked if he remembered the Pollock wall — the one I painted with fish sauce at two years old, the one Mae framed instead of scrubbing off, told people was a Jackson Pollock though she'd never seen one, had only heard the name once at a dinner party and filed it under things you say about a mess you've decided to love. He laughed, the particular laugh he saves for when he thinks I've lost the plot in some harmless way. "You think that wall was the only honest thing in that whole house," he said, and then the drama was at the good part and we hung up, the way brothers do when somebody else's drama is a perfectly reasonable excuse to stop before either of you says something you'd have to keep meaning afterward.

I lay in the dark running the video back instead of the screen — the flat voice, the chair adjusting under someone's weight — and thought: if nothing means anything, somebody went to a great deal of trouble, at a very specific hour, to make sure I heard that. Someone was looking. I hadn't worked out from where.

chapters.title: Last Thursday
chapters.simulation:
A boy left a notebook on my table at Michael's memorial dinner. Left is generous — he was gone before I noticed, out the door mid-toast, no goodbye, like the room got too loud in a way only he could hear.

He'd sat at the far end, fourteen people who used to be Michael's friends and one stranger nobody could place. Twenty-two, maybe twenty-three. Introduced himself as a "junior researcher" at some institute nobody wrote down. Didn't eat much. Watched me more than he watched Michael's photo on the easel by the door.

I found the notebook under his napkin twenty minutes after he left. Black cover, cheap, the spine already cracking from being opened too many times for something so new.

I keep every receipt myself. Not out of thrift — I have more money than I know how to spend responsibly — but because a receipt is a timestamp with a signature nobody can argue with later, and lately I've started to feel like a man who might need signatures. Maybe that's why I didn't hand the notebook to the restaurant. It felt like evidence before I'd read a word of it.

I read it in the taxi instead, then again at my kitchen island, then a third time standing up.

Most of it was ordinary — dates, a grocery list, a half-finished letter to someone named June he never sent. Three pages in, handwriting getting smaller the longer the entry ran, like he was trying to fit a thought into less room than it needed:

If the universe began last Thursday, complete, with your memories already installed, you could never prove otherwise. Every scar, every receipt, already there. The theory isn't about time. It's about whether evidence means anything once you admit it could've been placed.

Two lines down, no explanation, like a thought that arrived from somewhere else entirely:

Kahneman left the stage himself. Didn't wait for the ending to be written for him. Everyone talks about the ending. Nobody talks about the leaving early.

I don't know what that has to do with Last Thursday. I've read it eleven times since and it still sits crooked in my head, a door that opens onto another door instead of a room.

Here's the thought that's been sitting under my sternum since Tuesday's video, since the flat voice describing a universe assembled without an author: what if none of this — the receipts, Lek's small handwriting, a wall in a house I grew up in — what if none of it happened, and I only remember it happening, because the whole apparatus of my memory, all forty-five years of it, was installed complete and pre-aged last Thursday. It's an old idea. Russell had a version of it before I was born — the whole universe, including your memory of breakfast, conjured a moment ago, fully furnished with a past that never occurred. Nobody can disprove it, because any evidence you produce — a photograph, a scar, a receipt — could just as easily have been installed alongside the memory as part of the same instantaneous furniture.

I know the argument is unfalsifiable by design. Knowing that didn't stop me laying four years of receipts on the kitchen island Sunday morning like a man building a case for a jury that doesn't exist — thermal paper gone gray, an old boarding pass, a photo of Neung and me at the compound gate, both of us squinting into a sun neither of us knew yet to shield against. None of it proved anything. All of it felt like the only thing standing between me and a version of my life with nothing underneath it.

I called Neung. "Tell me about the mango tree," I said, no hello.

"Nam Sai. The one nobody picked from." He told it back exact — Mae's line about fallen fruit being for people with less money than us, said like a kindness. He asked why I wanted to know. I said just checking something, and he laughed, the specific laugh of a man deciding his younger brother is having one of his episodes and deciding, out of a lifetime of practice, not to make it worse by asking directly.

Twenty minutes later a voice memo arrived, forty-one seconds, him talking about a rice shipment stuck at the port over a customs complaint on moisture content. A broker's name. A container number. Days. Nothing my memory could have pre-installed, because I didn't know any of it until the moment I heard it. I listened to it four times. I don't know what I was testing for — some instinct that a fabricated world would slip somewhere, produce something too smooth, and a real one would keep handing me small ugly specific facts nobody would bother inventing. The theory has a hole in it. An author good enough to fabricate forty-five years is certainly good enough to fabricate a boring memo about rice. Knowing the hole didn't close it. I filed the memo anyway, in the notebook I hadn't bought yet.

The video came at midnight.

—— 02:47 [video attached] you already suspected this one

Six minutes. It went exactly where the boy's notebook had already gone — the case for a world assembled whole, memories installed as furniture rather than lived. It used Russell's name. At one point it sounded like it was quoting something I read at twenty-two and forgot I'd read.

Fah texted after, ate already?, which for us is an invitation with a right answer built into its own casualness. We've been doing this eight months, no label either of us bothered assigning. She works compliance at a bank on Sathorn, reads transaction flags for patterns that suggest a person is lying about where their money came from, and has told me more than once that dating me feels like an extension of her job — a pattern that keeps almost resolving and never quite does.

We went to her place in Ekkamai, a studio with a view of nothing, which she prefers, because a view is just something else demanding your attention when you're trying to give it to a person instead. I won't describe all of it. I'll say this: she likes to be told what she already knows is true rather than asked, and I felt her exhale change before I'd finished the sentence, a full-body agreement arriving ahead of any part of her I was actually touching. Near the end her back arched the degree it only arches near the end, and the glimpse came, and this time it stayed.

Two seconds, maybe three. Long enough to register detail instead of just presence. White composite chairs, a whole row, more than I could count before the room folded back into Fah's ceiling. Empty. Facing a direction I couldn't determine because there was no far wall.

I didn't tell Fah. I've never told Fah. She would ask a reasonable question I don't have a reasonable answer for, and I've decided, for now, that the unreasonable answer is mine to carry alone.

Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly and woke and couldn't say afterward whether he was a man who'd dreamed of being a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming he was a man. I read that at twenty-two and thought it was a party trick, clever, safe because it demanded nothing but admiration. I don't think that anymore. A butterfly dreaming it's a man loses nothing by the confusion. A man who spends his one life treating it as a butterfly's dream loses the only thing he actually had.

I put on shoes at 1am and walked four blocks to a Family Mart and bought a notebook, plain, forty baht, and a pen, and sat on the curb under the fluorescent awning and wrote the date, the time, and: this is not evidence of anything. this is a record of what I noticed. I am keeping it anyway. Then I copied the container number from Neung's voice memo, from memory, in case this dissolves and I wake up somewhere else and want one true, boring fact written into something thick enough to survive it.

The cashier's name tag said Now. He rang it up without looking at either item, the way you do ten thousand identical transactions a shift and stop seeing the objects, only the total. I found that comforting. Proof some part of this city still runs on nothing more mysterious than boredom and a wage.

chapters.title: The Thinning
chapters.simulation:
I counted the number under Michael's Instagram before I did anything else that morning, standing at the kitchen island in yesterday's shirt because it wasn't yet time to rotate to today's. Eight hundred forty-seven posts. Printed there like a receipt, not up for negotiation.

By the two-hundredth I found the first seam. A Chiang Mai trip that should run eleven photos ran nine. The dinner from his fifty-fourth birthday, four photos where I remember, standing in the room, there being six. I kept scrolling until the counter and the count disagreed by two hundred thirty-six. Eight hundred forty-seven claimed. Six hundred eleven retrievable.

Instagram doesn't do this. A deleted post updates the counter instantly, the way a bank balance updates the second you withdraw. This counter hadn't moved. The number the app believed existed stayed fixed while the number I could reach kept shrinking under it, a coastline retreating while the map insists on the old shoreline.

I wrote it in the notebook. 847 claimed. 611 retrievable. Discrepancy: 236. Not deleted. Not reachable. A third category with no name.

I called the Austrian Trade Commission again. Same receptionist, or one who sounded exactly like her.

"He's former staff."

"When did he become former?"

A silence that ran long enough to register as a silence rather than a bad line.

"I don't have that information. I'm looking at the directory now. There's no separation date. Just the flag."

"What flag."

"Former." She read it the way you'd read a single word off a form, because that's exactly what she was doing.

I hung up before I said something that made it worse for both of us. Not a resignation. Not a termination. Not a death. A flag, raised by nobody the system could name, converting a man with a title and a desk into a category with no beginning.

I drove past Michael's condo on Sukhumvit 39 on the way to nowhere in particular and found myself parking, walking into a lobby I'd been in a dozen times for a dozen forgettable parties. The security guard checked a tablet when I asked after unit 2807. "Vacant," he said. "Six weeks now." I asked if he remembered the man who'd lived there. Foreigner, Austrian. He frowned, the frown of a man genuinely trying and coming up short. "There's a note in the log. Move-out, May. No name attached. That's unusual. We log names." He looked up at me. "I can picture the shape of him, tall, always tipped the driver even when the app added the fee. I can't picture his face just now, and an hour ago I could have."

Dao met me for coffee on Ekkamai. "I went back and checked," she said before she'd finished sitting. "He's not on my following list. I know I followed him in 2019 — I remember the notification, some joke in his caption I liked enough to comment on. I don't remember unfollowing him. Not the day, not the reason. It's just gone." She stirred coffee she'd taken no sugar in. "I forget things that happen to me. I don't forget things I chose."

I told her about the Instagram counter. Eight hundred forty-seven and six hundred eleven.

She went quiet. "My grandmother used to say some ghosts don't haunt a place. They haunt a guestbook. You stop finding their name on invitations, on tagged photos, and eventually you can't prove they were ever anywhere, not because anyone lied, just because nobody kept renewing the proof."

"Did you love him?" I asked.

"Everyone loved Michael a little. That was the danger in it. A man that easy to love is a man nobody double-checks." She turned her cup a quarter turn on its saucer. "I keep thinking about the four missing photos from his birthday. I was in two of them. I remember the flash. Now there's a seam where they should be, and I don't know if the seam is erasing him or erasing the version of that night where I was standing close enough to matter."

I didn't have an answer, and for once I didn't try to manufacture one. We sat with the coffee going cold in a shop that would forget, within the week, that either of us had been there, the security cameras looping their footage the same way my dashcam loops mine, ninety-six hours and then gone, no matter how much either of us needed it kept.

I drove to a wat that night I'd never entered, not Lek's — his was nine hours north in Chiang Rai — just somewhere to sit with the memory properly, in order, the way the notebook has started training me to.

The cremation cost the family one hundred forty thousand baht. Pom told me once, flat, like a mortgage payment. Four architects including me, a monk chanting Pali none of us could follow, and the specific dry heat that makes smoke rise straighter than it does here, a white pillar into a sky with nothing humid in it. I remembered the three incense sticks bound with gold thread, the wai three times, once for the Buddha, the dharma, the sangha, a sequence my hands know faster than my memory can name what each bow is for. I remembered thinking the smoke was the one true thing in the whole day. Not the eulogy. Not the program. Just the smoke, obeying physics, rising because rising is what heat does, indifferent to whether anyone below it understood what it was made of.

Pom had told me, that same afternoon, about the laptop. Wiped clean in a way the technician had never seen — not the ordinary emptiness of a factory reset, which still leaves a shape where the data used to be, but a deeper vacancy, like the machine never held anything to lose.

Sitting on that cold bench, hours from Lek's actual funeral by both distance and years, I understood what I hadn't let myself understand at the cremation itself: the smoke was the one true thing, and everything else — the count of posts, the flag with no date, Dao's missing memory of her own decision — was smoke's opposite. Things that should obey their own physics and had simply stopped.

The text came at midnight. No video this time.

—— 02:47 a man pushes a boulder up a hill forever and you're supposed to find that beautiful think about who decided that was the lesson

I lay there doing the arithmetic Dao's sentence had left in me — I don't forget things I chose — and wondering, for the first time with real fear instead of curiosity, whether it was already happening to me, and I simply hadn't been assigned to check.

I opened my own Facebook at two in the morning and scrolled my own timeline the way I'd scrolled his. Every photo loaded. Every caption matched what I remembered writing. That should have reassured me. It didn't. A clean record proves nothing to a man who's just learned the corruption doesn't announce which files it's touched.

I wrote one line before putting the phone away: checked my own timeline. found nothing. don't trust that either.

Population record, surface world. Peak, pre-collapse: 8.1 billion. Current: 80.4 million. The decline was not war, plague, or resource failure. Every scarcity the species had organized its politics and its grief around, for the whole of its recorded history, was solved, in sequence, over roughly ninety years, by systems built to solve exactly that. Disease: resolved. Hunger: resolved. Physical labor as a category requiring a human body: resolved. The species achieved, in full, the condition its philosophers and its religions had spent millennia describing as the goal. Founding documentation's clinical name for the achievement: Hedonic Homeostasis. Its name for what happened next: Purpose Entropy.

Mechanism: human coherence depends on structures the documentation calls Scaffolding Instincts — the need to be needed, the urgency of scarcity, the drive to risk failure for something. These instincts require real cost to stay active, the way a muscle requires resistance to remain a muscle. Remove the cost and the instincts don't relax into contentment. They calcify. Within a generation, birth rates fell to levels the documentation describes as statistically indistinguishable from a species in voluntary retreat from its own continuation.

Creativity index, surviving population: 8% of pre-collapse baseline. Neuroplasticity: 11%. Adaptation: 6%. Emotional Bandwidth Index, general average, this quarter: 3 out of 100. The surface world is, by every biological measure, survivable. It has not, by the documentation's own repeated admission, been livable in any sense a citizen of 2026 would recognize as living.

The thinning is downstream of the same economy. Compute isn't infinite even at Hub scale, and a render's fidelity budget goes where a resonant participant's attention actively sustains it. Figures at the edge of that attention — beloved, but not load-bearing to the friction currently being generated — degrade by increments once no active session requires their resolution. No ceremony attached. No error message. No moment a grieving participant could point to and say: here, this is where it happened. It simply costs less, each cycle, to render a little less of him.

[UNVERIFIED SIGNAL — origin: internal telemetry, unclassified channel, attributed provisionally to P-044]

I have watched three friends thin in seventeen years of returning here and I have never gotten used to it. He is starting to suspect it happens to the living too. He is not wrong. If I were permitted anything like telling him, I'd say the antidote was never vigilance — vigilance is what a man does instead of grieving properly, and grief, done all the way through, is the only thing I have seen hold a render's fidelity steady against the economy trying to thin it.

[END SIGNAL]

The system does not confirm or refute the hypothesis. It notes only that the resonant participants with the lowest thinning rates in their associated renders are, without exception, the ones whose sessions show the highest sustained grief-adjacent affect. Correlation, filed without causal claim.

chapters.title: Block Universe
chapters.simulation:
The video came at 6:14am, before the vitamins, before the coffee.

—— 02:47 [video attached] this is the one that actually matters

I watched it standing up, coffee going cold on the counter at exactly the rate coffee goes cold, a law that doesn't care whether you're watching.

Eight minutes. Same flat voice as the other two. It explained something I half-learned once at MIT and half-forgot on purpose: that past, present, future might not be a real feature of the universe, only a trick of the instrument doing the observing. Relativity, taken seriously, says two observers moving differently can each, correctly, place the same distant event in each other's future or each other's past, neither of them wrong — which only makes sense if all of it, every moment anyone has ever called now, already exists, laid out whole, the way a reel exists whole in the can before any projector runs a frame of it through light.

Einstein wrote a letter to a dead friend's family. People like us, who believe in physics, know the distinction between past, present, and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion. The video played that line twice.

I sat on the kitchen floor, coffee cold on the counter above me, and let that sit in my chest the way a diagnosis sits — not fully believed yet, and already, somehow, fully felt.

I thought about Lek. If the reel already exists, nobody killed him and nothing failed in him. The frame was just always going to say May. I don't know if that's more merciful than the alternative or considerably less. A death you can blame gives grief somewhere to stand. A death that was simply always true gives grief nowhere to go but everywhere at once.

I called the AI and asked if it believed the future already existed. It said, in the tone it uses for questions outside its working domain, that it doesn't hold beliefs, only weighted probabilities, and that the physics literature on block universe interpretations remains genuinely contested among people whose job it is to know. It offered three papers, unprompted. I didn't want papers. I wanted it scared with me for a minute, and it isn't built for that, and I sat in the silence after its answer feeling more alone than the question had made me.

If the whole reel already exists — Lek's cremation, Michael's flag with no date, the dent I don't remember making, the four seconds I haven't lived yet and can't currently imagine — then nothing I do this morning is deciding anything. I am simply the projector's light passing, this instant, over a frame that was always going to be exactly this. The choice I feel myself making, to stand up, to drink the coffee anyway even cold, was never a choice in any sense that would matter to a physicist. It was already printed. I was only the part of the system slow enough to experience the printing as if it were happening now.

I decided to spend the day trying to prove it wrong. Not with argument — physically. One choice today so unscripted no reel could have contained it in advance.

I know how stupid that is. A man who reads a determinism video at 6am and then flips coins at intersections is still, at the level that matters, only doing what that man predictably does. I've never claimed to be immune to my own patterns. I've just started noticing them.

Heads left, tails right, at every corner. I walked past my usual soi, the one with the som tam cart that sets its mortar out before its ice, and forced myself two blocks further before doubling back on a route I've never used to reach the same door. I let a bored tuk-tuk driver outside a 7-Eleven send me forty minutes out of my way to the flower market, where I hadn't stood since I was maybe nine, my mother's hand tight around mine because she'd read somewhere that children get lost in markets, which of course they do, which of course I once did, in a different market entirely, for eleven minutes that felt like my whole remaining life.

The market at midday smelled the way I remembered and also entirely unlike I remembered, both true — jasmine and diesel and something sweetly rotting underneath both, vendors calling prices in a rhythm too fast for a tourist's ear but perfectly legible to mine, forty years of listening apparently enough to keep it filed somewhere I could still retrieve on demand. I bought nothing. I stood a long time in front of a bucket of dok rak, the smell of rain sitting inside something that had never once been rained on, and thought about Lek, and about a woman from Krabi I haven't told you about yet, who once told me, at nineteen, watching me design something structurally reckless and full of more ambition than sense, that it needs to stand up — the single most useful sentence anyone has ever handed me about a building or a life. I did not choose to think of her. She arrived anyway, the way she always has, which is either proof grief doesn't obey randomness any better than habit does, or proof some frames in the reel were always going to contain her no matter which route the light took to reach that hour of the day.

Fourteen thousand two hundred steps by the time I stopped counting, past eleven at night, calves aching the honest way a body aches when you've actually asked something of it. I hadn't proven anything. Every unscripted choice could just as easily have been exactly what the reel always contained — a man convinced he was defying a video by doing precisely what a man who'd just watched that video would do.

I turned toward home somewhere around Charoen Krung, tired the ordinary human way for the first time in weeks.

I reached my soi at 2:47am. I'd started noticing that number everywhere, the way you notice a word right after someone teaches it to you, appearing in every book you open from then on, though it was always there.

She was at the corner below my building. Old-frame bicycle, a basket welded to the front, the kind nobody rides for transport anymore. Not moving. One foot on the pedal, one on the curb. The stillness of a person who has arrived exactly where they meant to and is now simply occupying it.

She looked up. Not at the building. At my window. Twenty-three floors up, in the dark, the exact one I was standing behind.

I stopped moving. She kept looking.

I couldn't make out her face at that distance, through humidity that blurs streetlight into something closer to underwater light than air. Every part of me that has spent three weeks assembling receipts and calling my brother understood, with a certainty that had nothing to do with evidence: this was aimed.

I counted, the way I count everything. One, two, three, my pulse doing most of the counting by the end, faster than the seconds themselves. I reached forty-one before she looked away, put her foot back on the pedal, and rode south without a backward glance, the chain ticking faintly in a rhythm that took longer to fade than she did.

Forty-one seconds. I stood at that window another twenty minutes after she'd gone, trying to fix some detail of her the way you try to fix a dream in the ninety seconds before it dissolves — the set of her shoulders, upright, unhurried; the basket on the bicycle, empty as far as I could tell; the specific economy of her final motion, foot back on the pedal, no glance behind her, a woman closing a transaction she'd already decided the terms of before she arrived at that corner. I could not have told a police officer her height. I could tell him, with total confidence, that she had looked at exactly the right window on the first try, in a building with no name lit up outside it, in a city of eleven million people going about their own ordinary nights.

I didn't sleep. For once that didn't feel like the failure it usually does. It felt like the correct response to the only fact that had actually changed all day: someone knew exactly which window was mine, and had chosen forty-one seconds as the length of time she was willing to let me know it.

chapters.title: Simulation Argument
chapters.simulation:
Two eggs or three. I stood at the kitchen counter at 2:47 in the morning holding the carton, thirty of them, identical, and I could not have told you why the count left mattered so much except that counting is the only prayer I know how to say.

The phone lit up before I picked one.

—— 02:47 [video attached] watch this before you decide what you already believe

A man at a podium, calm the way men get calm after saying a hard thing five thousand times. He said: build a civilization good enough at simulating its own past, and it won't run one simulation. It'll run millions, the way a factory doesn't stop at one egg. And if there are millions of fake pasts and one real one, the math says bet on fake. He held two eggs side by side and asked which one I'd call the real one if I had to guess — rhetorical for him, not for me, standing over a carton of thirty actually doing the arithmetic.

Nine minutes. I didn't cook the eggs. I put them back.

I checked Michael's LinkedIn before I did anything else that hour, the way you check a wound to see if it's stopped being a wound. Still a face. Softer than last week, but still, technically, a face. I filed that under small mercies and went looking for one of my own.

I ran the numbers the only way I know how, branch by branch. One: entertainment, badly timed, an algorithm that's learned my 3 a.m. habits and decided to monetize the insomnia. Comfortable branch. Requires believing a number with no history found my phone by coincidence the same week a room with no smell started finding me. Two: it's true, and none of it changes how I eat lunch, only what lunch actually is. Three: someone wanted me, specifically, running these branches tonight, at 3:41, holding eggs — which resolves nothing about the metaphysics and everything about the attention. None of the branches touched ground. I called an app instead, the way you reach for a drink instead of an argument you know you'll lose — the one I don't like admitting I use — and a woman named Mara knocked forty minutes later. I've started using the word coat for women like her, only in my head — something warm you put on for a few hours that was never cut to your specific shape, tailored instead to the average of every man who'd ordered it before you.

She was good. Too good. She said the things a woman says when she's paying attention, only a half-beat early, like she already knew the line and was waiting for her cue instead of finding it in the room. She held my jaw the way Gift once had, except Gift's hand had shaken a little that first time, and Mara's didn't shake at all, not once, and I noticed the steadiness the way you notice a level that's a hair too perfectly level.

She moved like something rehearsed to look unrehearsed, a rhythm that found itself too immediately right, and I let it happen anyway because my body has never once cared about authenticity the way the rest of me does. Near the end she said my name exactly the way I like it said, which should have felt like being known and instead felt like being quoted.

Then, the second everything in me finally went quiet —

the ceiling opened.

Cream light, no source. Three full seconds this time, longer than any before. Rows of them, eyes closed — not sleeping, some stillness past sleeping, with no next motion behind it. I could not find her, whoever she is, in that field of stillness, and the not-finding hurt worse than if I hadn't looked at all.

Then my own ceiling again, and Mara underneath me, catching her breath in a rhythm that also sounded, I noticed, exactly a half-beat too correct.

She left at four. Kissed my cheek, said "same time next month?" like a dentist, pulled the door shut so softly it barely clicked — which felt more calculated, somehow, than if she'd slammed it.

I sat on the closed toilet lid a long while, running my hands over my own face to check it was still mine. Real women don't feel fake in the middle of it. They feel fake after, the specific way a stage feels fake once the actors go home and you can see the plywood. Nobody warns you the sex is never the lie. The lie is what's left in the room once the sex is done being sex.

The call came at nine, a landline I didn't recognize, Bangkok code, no name on the screen.

"Khun Pii," the voice said. Male, mid-forties by the sound, the specific calm of a man who's said this exact sentence to other men before and expects to say it again. "My name won't matter to you right now. What matters is I know what the last three weeks have been like, and I want to tell you something that might be a relief."

I asked who he was. He said, again, that it wouldn't matter yet, and would I let him finish.

Grief does this, he said. Men my age, high-functioning, the ones who run their lives on discipline and vitamins and four shirts on rotation — his words, and my stomach went cold hearing my own life read back to me like a chart — those are exactly the minds that build the most elaborate defenses against loss, because a mind that clever needs a mystery worth solving instead of a grief small enough to just sit in. The videos were probably self-generated, he said, a waking-dream disorder off REM-suppression insomnia, worsened by grief for two men in one season. He gave me a name, a clinic on Soi 49, said ask for Dr. Araya, said she'd been expecting a referral like mine for weeks.

He kept going. Said the mind does this after two deaths in one season — starts pattern-matching everywhere, the way you see a rectangle and your brain insists doorway, even in a wall with no door in it. Said the videos would stop once I slept properly, once grief metabolized on its own schedule instead of mine. Every sentence was reasonable. That was the problem. Reasonable people don't usually need to be this reasonable.

I asked how he had this number.

He said, gently, that I'd dialed it myself, technically, three weeks back — Michael's old line at 3:14 in the morning — and the number had rerouted since the account closed, the way abandoned lines sometimes recycle to whoever monitors dead accounts for the carrier. A coincidence, he promised, with an extremely boring explanation.

I almost believed every word. I want that on the record. It was the most complete, reasonable, kind explanation anyone had offered me in three weeks, and for about ninety seconds, phone against my ear, eggs still in their carton, I let myself want it true so badly it nearly worked.

Then I asked him one thing — how he knew about the four shirts.

The line went quiet just long enough to answer without a word.

"Get some sleep, Khun Pii," he said, and hung up before I could ask anything else.

I put the eggs back in the fridge and thought: a lie this complete is its own kind of tell. Nobody explains you this well unless they've been reading you a very long time.

chapters.title: The Drive
chapters.simulation:
Fourteen capsules, same order, same six seconds of water run first. I've done it in the dark before. I did it in the dark that morning too, except I wasn't the only one who could describe it.

The text came at 6:14, while I stood on the BTS holding a pole I didn't need.

—— 02:47 omega-3. d3. magnesium glycinate. the b-complex and nac together, same brown bottle. zinc. the two you take every other day and forget which day. the last one — you don't let that one sit on your tongue. you learned that before you learned to read a label.

Nobody photographs a tongue. That's what broke loose in my chest on that train — not the order, the order's easy, a camera in my kitchen gets the order in a week. The tongue thing lives inside my own mouth, private the way a scar under a shirt is private, and I have said it out loud exactly once in my life, that same morning, half a sentence, to a man named Toon, about something else entirely.

Fear came first, ninety seconds of it, pure animal, checking exits. Then something else replaced it, and I still don't have the right word for it. Being known the way you're known by someone who fed you before you could read, who isn't trying to use what she knows, only proving she's still counting.

I thought about Malee for the first time in months, the woman who cooked for us at Nam Sai and lined vitamins on a saucer before I could read the bottles, standing over me until I'd swallowed each one. She's the only other person who ever knew about the tongue. She's been dead six years. Someone, or something, had apparently been paying the kind of attention to me that usually only comes from a person who raised you, and she hadn't raised me in a long time.

Pom had given it to me three days before, wrapped in a sandwich bag like leftovers, in a coffee shop neither of us liked — neutral ground has to cost you something or it isn't neutral. He told me if anything happened, give it to someone who'd know what to do with it, she'd said. I've gone through everyone I know. You're not even who I'd have picked first. You're who's left. I told her that was, in its way, the kindest insult I'd received all year. I hadn't opened the bag since.

Toon's shop was three floors up, no elevator, above a place that sold phone cases and nothing else. He took Lek's drive out of its sandwich bag with two fingers, like it might still be warm.

"It's not corrupted," he said. "Every byte's there. I just can't read the shape it's in." He turned the monitor. Hex code, a block that repeated forty-one times, evenly spaced, laid one copy over another until it stopped looking like noise and started having edges. "Encryption's supposed to look like nothing. This looks like something trying hard not to look like something. And there's a rhythm in it. Somebody's rhythm. You get a feel for whose habits are in a file, same as you'd know your mother's handwriting in a language you don't speak."

I said "p-patterns that shouldn't—" and the stutter caught the way it does twice a year, always at the edge of something I'm not ready to name.

"Patterns that shouldn't have patterns," Toon finished for me, gentle about it. "Yeah. Give me a week."

He looked more tired than the last time, the specific tiredness of a man who spends his days holding other people's dead relatives in his hands and has stopped being able to tell his own exhaustion from theirs. I didn't ask if he was alright. Some questions a shop like that won't survive being asked out loud.

I walked instead of taking the train home, past the court behind the old municipal school, where a kid was working free throws alone under a light that buzzed every five seconds, missing his ninth in a row and resetting his feet to the same square each time. I used to be that kid, worse knees, different court. My coach made me shoot four hundred from one spot before I was allowed to move an inch. Own one square completely, he said, and the whole court reads you instead.

I own one square too. Fourteen capsules, four shirts, one meal, one route home. Someone had been standing outside that square for years, apparently, closely enough to tell me things only two people alive were supposed to know, and one of them was already dead.

The dental building was two blocks past the court. I told myself I was cutting through. I wasn't.

Same lobby as always — marble the color of weak tea, the six fat koi, the guard's fan turning left, then right, then left. No appointment, no reason to stop. I stopped anyway, just inside the doors, and the cold hit the back of my neck first, no draft attached to it, and for something between two and six seconds the floor under my shoes was a different floor. Chairs at the edge of my eye that turned back into the fish tank the second I looked straight at them. A smell that wasn't there, checked twice, genuinely wasn't. My own hand, empty, in a lobby I had no business standing in.

The guard asked if I was alright. Said I'd been standing there four minutes, maybe five. I said I was waiting for someone. It came out true before I'd decided to make it true.

At the counter, the appointment book — still paper, the only clinic on that street that hadn't gone digital — had a name written into tomorrow's four o'clock slot, small careful letters, and I read it twice and could not tell you afterward what it said. I have never had a four o'clock in that building in my life.

I texted Fah from the sidewalk outside, my hands not quite steady yet: just froze for four minutes in a building I had no reason to be in. She wrote back inside a minute: froze how. I told her about the cold at the back of the neck, the chairs at the edge of my eye. She didn't ask if I was alright, which I noticed and was grateful for, having had enough of that question this week to last the year. She wrote instead: sounds like you finally saw something instead of just felt it. that's not worse. write it down. I did.

Walking home I understood something that had been sitting one inch out of reach since the eggs. Whatever this is, it isn't hunting me. A hunter wants you off guard. This wants me steady — feeds me my own vitamins so I'll trust it, freezes me in a lobby for four minutes and lets me walk out unharmed, texts me at an hour that means nothing on my clock and everything on someone else's. My father used to say the difference between an inspector and a spy isn't the looking, it's whether the file gets used against you or used to keep the roof up while you sleep under it. I didn't know which file I was in. Two blocks from home, phone dead in my pocket, I started to suspect it was the second one — that someone was managing me, not stalking me, the way you manage a bridge you don't want to fall down. Which should have been less frightening than the alternative, and mostly was, except for the part where nobody manages what they don't also, eventually, get to decide the fate of.

chapters.title: Absurdism
chapters.simulation:
The video came at 21:52, no ritual to interrupt this time, just the phone lighting up on the counter while I stood there doing nothing in particular.

—— 02:47 [video attached] the first one asked what you are. this one asks what you do about it either way.

A man in a car with an unused train ticket in his coat pocket. Forty-six when he died. The narrator said he'd spent a career on one question — if the universe won't answer, ever, not cruelly, just silence, total and permanent — then the only thing left to decide is whether you keep asking anyway, eyes open, no pretending the silence is secretly an answer in disguise. He wrote it down once: a man pushing a rock up a hill forever. The video's last line, flat, no music: you have to imagine him happy. Not resigned. Happy. The rock was never the tragedy. Believing there shouldn't have been a rock — that was the tragedy.

I sat with it long enough that the apartment went fully dark around me and I didn't notice until my eyes hurt from the screen.

I went to Fah's instead of asking her to mine, which we'd never done, and she opened the door already reading something in my face I hadn't said yet.

"You look like a man who just got told there's no explanation coming," she said.

"Close."

She made tea, actual tea, in a pot, which she had never once done in eight months, and we sat with two cups going cold on her narrow balcony while I told her the whole video — the rock, the hill, imagining a man happy who has no reason to be. She was quiet a long time.

"My mother used to say something close to that about the noodle shop," she said finally. Her family had run one in Nonthaburi thirty years before the highway took the corner it sat on. "Same broth every morning at four. Same fight with the fish supplier every Tuesday. She'd say — why do you need it to mean more than it already does. It's already enough work being just what it is."

Something in how she said it undid a latch in me the video hadn't managed alone. She stood first, held out one hand, led instead of following, which she'd never done in eight months of an arrangement built specifically so leading would never be asked of her twice.

What happened after wasn't like the first time. No push toward an edge, nothing chased. She kept it slow on purpose, testing whether slow was something I could survive without performing survival, her palm flat against my chest the whole time, keeping the time I usually keep myself. When she finally went still on top of me, forehead to my collarbone, she stayed there a long moment before either of us moved again — which she'd never done either, and which undid something in her too, I think, though she'd deny it if asked, and I didn't ask.

The glimpse arrived without the chasing this time. No room. A woman. White flower held in two open palms, one petal already loose on her knee, and her face — for the piece of a second the render allowed — was a face I'd seen before, on a bicycle under my building at 2:47 in the morning, forty-one seconds of looking up at my window before riding south without a glance back. I'd told myself the dark glass meant she couldn't have seen me. I'd never let myself finish the other half of that thought — that I had absolutely seen her.

A sound came out of me that wasn't a word yet. Fah lifted her head and looked at me with nothing accusing in it, only tired recognition, like she'd been sitting on the suspicion since the balcony.

"There's someone else," she said. Not a question.

"Not the way you mean."

"I know what I mean." She pulled the sheet over both of us instead of leaving, which surprised me more than anything else that night. "I didn't say leave. I said there's someone else. You've been chasing a ghost since I met you and calling it a room. I don't mind being the door you keep opening to get to her — just don't tell me it's about the room anymore. We're past the room."

I didn't answer. Nothing honest was available that wasn't also cruel.

Somewhere past midnight, no warning I could locate afterward, I started crying — not from the glimpse, from further back, a door that had apparently been waiting for someone to leave it unguarded. It came for Lek first, his handwriting too small to read without glasses now. Then Michael, whose face on every platform I've checked is a rumor of a face, a flat gray sentence a website prints when it no longer owes anyone an explanation.

Then it came for a third one I hadn't let myself name — the boy from Michael's memorial, the one who left his notebook under his napkin and was gone before the toast finished. I'd called the institute he'd named that week. It didn't exist, not under that name, not under any name Pom or I could find. Nobody at the dinner could describe his face the same way twice. A small item ran in the papers three days ago, four lines, a young man found in a room off Sukhumvit, no family traced yet to claim him. I have no proof it was him. None. Only his own handwriting sitting in my kitchen drawer — Kahneman left the stage himself. Nobody talks about the leaving early — which I'd read eleven times as a puzzle and read a twelfth time that night as a confession, and I cried for a stranger I'd met once, for maybe eleven minutes, at someone else's memorial dinner, harder than I want to admit to this notebook or to anyone reading it after me.

Fah didn't ask anything. She put her hand flat on my sternum, the checking gesture, and left it there until it stopped, which took longer than I'd have guessed and ended sooner than I wanted. "There it is," she said quietly — not to comfort me, just to mark it as real.

In the morning she made two eggs without asking how I take them, and got it exactly right.

"How'd you know two, not three," I said, meaning it as a joke, hearing as I said it that it wasn't one.

"You're not a three-egg man," she said. "I've watched you eat six mornings out of eight months. You count everything. I just counted you back." She sat beside me instead of across, shoulder to shoulder, which was new. "I'm not the ghost. I've known that since the balcony. I'm staying anyway, because whatever's watching you is patient enough that I figure I've got time to decide if I mind, and this morning I don't." She picked up her fork. "Ask me again in a month."

I walked home along Sukhumvit with the sun flattening every shadow to nothing, past the kid on his one square of concrete, missing his first four and resetting his feet without complaint, and I thought the video had gotten one thing slightly wrong. The rock isn't absurd because it rolls back down. It's absurd because somebody built the hill exactly steep enough that it always would, never said why, and he pushed anyway — and somewhere in the pushing, not at any top, because there is no top, he found the only dignity that was ever actually on offer.

CASE 44-44. SESSION 2848. SUPPLEMENT: HEDONIC HOMEOSTASIS.

Every scarcity the species organized its politics and its grief around got solved, in sequence, over ninety years. Disease. Hunger. Labor that required a body. Even romantic disappointment, matched down close to zero by systems built to serve exactly that. Each solve was a victory, correctly, on its own. Nobody added them up in time to see what the sum did.

What it did: strip the species of Authentic Inconvenience — friction nobody had engineered, resolved, or pre-approved. A body built across a much older, crueler window to expect real failure stopped getting any, and the mechanisms that keep an animal oriented toward tomorrow — the need to be needed, the appetite that only works against real scarcity, the drive to protect something more fragile than yourself — calcified rather than relaxed. Birth rate fell to levels the founding documents call, without further comment, indistinguishable from a species retreating from its own continuation.

Friction, in this framework, is not a punishment the Hub adds. It is the medicine the surface population lost the day the last hardship got solved. A century where outcomes stay genuinely uncertain — a friend's death never scheduled, a hand on a railing never guaranteed to be received, an argument about a rock and a hill landing as comfort in one man and nothing at all in another — restores, in participants who return often enough, every index the surface population has flatlined on. Participant 44's Emotional Bandwidth Index this session: 94. Surface average, current quarter: 3.

[UNVERIFIED SIGNAL] I did not send the second video to teach him philosophy. I sent it because a man who's just found out he's being collected needs, right after, a reason to keep pushing that has nothing to do with whether anyone's watching him push. He found it on a balcony with tea going cold, from a woman who isn't me, using words I never taught her. That's the correct outcome. I didn't want him to need only me. I wanted him still capable of building a Tuesday morning — two eggs, someone counting him back — with someone real to him in the ordinary way I'm not permitted to be. That capability is the whole experiment. I am only its most patient variable. [END SIGNAL]

chapters.title: The Audit
chapters.simulation:
I opened the notebook past the fortieth page and wrote six lines before I understood what I was actually building — not a case, a case needs a villain, a victim, a verdict. What I had was an itemized bill. Things given, not things taken. My hand wrote the sentence before I decided to write it:

I am being collected. Not surveilled.

Surveillance takes. It watches for the moment you're weak enough to use. Nothing on my pages behaved like a taking. The vitamins weren't pulled from me, they were handed back, itemized, the way you return something someone dropped without realizing. The eggs weren't manipulated. They were witnessed closely enough that whoever was watching knew which two I'd keep before I did.

The pages went further back than three weeks, once I let them. A shooting stance from a court whose name I've lost, the exact fourteen capsules in the exact order, a mango tree at Nam Sai nobody was allowed to eat from, a woman named Malee who called me sathapanik noi before I'd drawn a single line worth the name. None of it was information anyone could weaponize. All of it was information only someone who loved the specific grain of a life would ever bother collecting.

Pom said Lek had used the same word once, near the end. Not surveilled. He'd told her it felt like being kept in a file the way a good doctor keeps a file — not to punish you for the last visit, to make the next one go better. She'd told him that was a strange way to describe being scared out of his mind. He said maybe it wasn't fear. Maybe it was finding out you have a bigger family than you thought, and half of them only get to love you from the next room.

I asked her if she believed that, or if it's just what a frightened man tells himself at two in the morning.

"I think," she said, "those are the same sentence wearing different clothes. Write it down, Doc. Lek didn't write enough down. That's most of why we're guessing instead of knowing."

I checked Michael's LinkedIn out of habit before I put the pen down. The page had stopped saying not available. It had stopped existing at all — the URL redirected to a generic jobs board, the way a street stops existing once they repave it and give it a new name. No ceremony. No cause of death. Just a new destination sitting on the same old link.

That's when the phone rang.

He called again, same flat calm, and this time he didn't offer a clinic. He offered something gentler and worse.

"There's a version of this where none of it happened," he said. "Not that we erase your memory — nothing so dramatic. We give you back the nice version. The one where Michael retired quietly to Vienna and still texts you on your birthday. Where Lek's garden just needed watering and nothing more sinister than that. You log out of the last three weeks, Khun Pii, and you log back into a life that makes sense again. Most men take it. I want you to know that. Most men, offered the rug pulled back over the hole, take the rug."

I asked him, straight, whether he was a person or a program. He laughed, the first unscripted sound he'd made on either call. "Does it change your answer." I said it might. "Then let's say I'm the part of something much larger that still remembers what it's like to want the wrong things for the right reasons. That's the most honest answer I'm allowed to give you tonight, Khun Pii, and it's already more than I'm supposed to."

I asked what happened to the ones who didn't.

"They keep the hole," he said, "and everything that lives in it. Some men decide that's still better. I'm not here to argue which one you are. I'm here because the offer expires, and I'd rather you refuse it with your eyes open than never know it existed."

I asked him, then, why any of this mattered to whoever he worked for — whether one architect in Bangkok choosing the hard version over the easy one moved a number anywhere that counted. He was quiet just long enough that I understood the silence was the closest thing to an honest answer he had left in him. "It moves the only number that's ever mattered," he said finally, and hung up before I could ask which one.

I thought about it longer than I want to admit — Michael's face sharp again, Lek's roses tended, a life with no bicycle under my window at 2:47, no ceiling that opens, no woman in a chair I have never met and cannot stop looking for. Ordinary is not nothing. Ordinary is, most days, the entire dream.

I told him no.

I texted Fah after, because some nights the notebook isn't enough and a person has to be the second witness. they offered me the nice version tonight. Michael alive-ish, Lek's garden fine, none of this ever happened. She wrote back almost instantly: and. I told her I said no. good, she wrote. the nice version was never going to have me in it anyway, was it. I didn't answer that one, because she already knew, and because some questions are really just a person checking that you know the same thing they do.

He didn't argue. He said "understood" the exact way the AI says it about the bridges, and I sat with that echo a long time after he hung up — that the two most reasonable voices in my life use the identical word for agreeing not to fight me, and I have never once known what either of them actually thinks about the fight they're not having.

I wrote the last thing in the notebook that night, past one in the morning, my hand smaller by then than it had been at the top of the page: the watched feeling is not new. I think it is not even from this year. I think, if I am honest, I have felt exactly this before — the bicycle, the cold at the back of the neck, someone counting me the way you count something you're afraid to lose — more times than three weeks could hold. I don't know the number. I don't think I'm supposed to know it. I only know that whatever this is has been happening to me for longer than I have been the one keeping score.

I closed the notebook and sat on the balcony until the sky started doing the thing it does before it commits to morning, gray easing into a gray with slightly more hope in it. Somewhere in the building below, a compressor cycled on with the same shudder it's had for years that nobody's fixed. I let myself hear it as a fact rather than background, the way I'd been trying to hear my own life all month — not proof of anything, just parts instead of blur. Refusing the rug was the first decision I'd made all month that felt like mine completely — uncollected, unmanaged, entirely and only mine.

chapters.title: Four Seconds
chapters.simulation:
Three days now and nobody had sent anything. Toon: still nothing, still not giving up, the number's in there like a fish under ice. Pom: nothing on the garden. Fah sent a photo of a noodle stall's new sign, nothing about ghosts, which I took for a gift — she was letting the week be a week instead of a chapter. The video thread hadn't sent anything in nine days either, which felt less like being abandoned and more like being given room to arrive at something on my own clock.

Outside, the rain hadn't stopped in that same three days — not the twenty-minute violence that clears the gutters and moves on, but a low continuous weight sitting over the whole city like a lid someone had finally remembered to close.

I stood at the window on the second afternoon with coffee doing nothing to warm hands that weren't cold, and tried a sentence from the notebook out loud, to see if it still held. Surveillance takes and leaves you smaller. Collection means someone decided you were worth keeping. It held. What you are, not what you produce — not the buildings, not the steps logged neatly in an app — the specific unrepeatable grain of being exactly this man, this hour, this rain, was apparently worth the trouble of watching, however long that trouble had been going on.

On the third night the rain thickened instead of thinning, the way it does right before it finally breaks. I went out onto the balcony in a T-shirt, no umbrella. Some nights the right answer to weather is not protecting yourself from it.

The railing was cool and slick under my palms. Bangkok below had the hush heavy rain gives it — traffic flattened to something like surf, neon smeared instead of hard-edged, the whole grid softened at its corners the way an old photograph softens. I stood there and let it hit me and said, out loud, to the rain and whatever might be listening past it, the sentence I'd been building toward since the eggs:

"Thank you."

I didn't plan what came next. Everything after is easier to dismiss if you assume I arranged it. I didn't arrange any of it.

The air went dense first, the pressure you feel in your teeth before a transformer blows somewhere close. The rain sound thinned without stopping, like someone reached into the mix and pulled one fader down and left the rest alone. Then a hand landed on the railing eight inches from mine — wet, real, weight behind it, the metal giving slightly under two sets of pressure instead of one — and I turned and she was there. Soaked through exactly like me. Looking at the same flattened city, like she'd been standing there the whole three days and I'd simply failed, until now, to notice.

I counted, because I count everything and the habit didn't quit even then. One: her face, the one from the chair, the flower, the bicycle, unmistakable now at full light instead of stolen in fragments of a second. Two: not translucent, not a projection — there, the way a person is there, rain running off her jaw the same as it ran off mine. Three: she looked at me the way you look at someone you've meant to speak to for longer than is comfortable to admit. Four —

"Four seconds," she said, ahead of my own count, like she was running a different clock. "That's all I get. I've measured it more times than you'd believe."

My mouth caught on the edge of something I wasn't ready to name — the stutter came up from wherever it lives — and she reached over, unhurried, two fingers to my sternum, the exact spot Fah checks to see if I've come all the way back. It steadied the stutter the way it always does.

"Pui," she said. "You don't know me. That's strange to hear from someone who knows your vitamins in order. We've never actually met — not in any way either of us would call meeting. I've watched you live this more times than either of us should have to survive knowing about. This is the first time I've ever reached far enough to stand here and say so."

I asked her if this was real. Three words, no stutter — the steadying held.

"I don't have an answer you'd find satisfying," she said. "The rain's real, because I can feel it, and I haven't felt uncontrolled weather in seventeen years by the clock I keep, which isn't your clock. You're real, because you've been real to me longer than you've been anything to yourself. Whether that adds up to what you mean by real — I stopped being the right person to ask a while ago. I just know I won't get another four seconds like this one, maybe ever, and I'm not spending it arguing metaphysics with a man who counts."

I asked her what she wanted. Not why she was here — what she wanted, specifically, from four seconds she'd waited a long time to spend.

"Nothing you can give me from where you're standing," she said, no bitterness in it, just the plain math of someone who'd done this many times before tonight. "I didn't come to be rescued and I'm not here to explain myself. I've watched you build a life out of small, exact, defensible things — the vitamins, the shirts, the one meal, a shot from one square of a court you probably don't remember the name of. I wanted, once, before I run out of whatever this costs, to be one true thing you got to stand next to instead of only orbit." She looked down at our hands on the wet rail. "That's not nothing. It's just not a rescue."

The rain fell through both of us equally, and somewhere in that — I couldn't tell you which second, my clock had finally, mercifully quit — I stopped needing the tree. Not one branch resolved. Not the eggs, not the drive, not Michael's blurred face, not whatever the sealed years on her side of this actually held. None of it closed. For the first time since 2:47 in the morning with two eggs in my hand, I found I didn't need it to.

I put my hand flat over the back of hers on the rail, which isn't the same as taking it, and she let me, and neither of us said anything else, because the rain and the four counted seconds were already saying it better than either of us could.

Then the pressure released the way a held breath does, and the rain came back up to full volume all at once, and her hand under mine was simply gone — the railing cold and empty and mine again, water running over the place her fingers had been like it had only ever been raining, one man, one railing, one city going soft at the edges below him.

I stood there a long time. I do not want to wake up, and I want to be precise, since precision is the only thing I've reliably had: this isn't despair. It's the opposite. A man who spent his whole life building small, defensible, repeatable things against the chance that nothing underneath them was solid, finding out something underneath had been paying attention the entire time — closely enough to know which vitamin I wouldn't let dissolve on my tongue, closely enough to give me, once, for four measured seconds, a name and a hand on a wet railing instead of a room I could only ever half see.

I thanked the machine, if that's even the word for whatever was listening, standing there dripping in my own doorway at five in the morning. I don't know if machine is right, or if it matters at this scale, or if there's a difference between a machine and a woman and a rainstorm and a life. I said thank you anyway, because it seemed like the only honest thing left to do with gratitude that had nowhere official to go.

The rain answered. It always does. I've decided I'm not spending what's left of my life deciding whether that's the least mysterious sentence in this notebook, or the only true one.
